newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius ex-finance chiefs slam budget.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius ex-finance chiefs slam budget.

text.p: Three opposition former finance ministers and economists said on Friday the Mauritius budget for 1997/98 is misguided and fails to address the key issues facing the Indian Ocean island's economy.
Finance Minister Vasant Bunwaree said in Monday's budget he would propose legislation on VAT in the next financial year to improve revenue and facilitate investment, but gave few details.

He also proposed a $97.2 million fund for socio-economic development funded by the sale of an as yet undisclosed stake in the government's Overseas Telecommunication Services Ltd and said he would scrap a levy on the important sugar industry introduced last year.
Rundheersing Bheenick, finance minister in 1996 for the Labour-MMM alliance government, said the lacked ambition and vision.
Rama Sithanen, finance minister in Aneerood Jugnauth's government from 1991 to 1995, said a philosophy of high expenditure and high taxes guided the budget.

"The budget contains excessive sale of prime assets to finance very high expenditure," he said, adding it was not certain how government would finance expenditure after exhausting revenue from privatisation.
Sithanen said the budget deficit for 1997/98 was estimated artificially at 3.3 billion rupees ($159.8 million).
Mauritius' budget deficit for the 1996/97 financial year would be 4.6 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Bunwaree said..

Total expenditure would amount to 21.3 billion rupees ($1,036.4 million) during the financial year 1996/97 while tol revenue would be 17.6 billion rupees, giving a budget deficit of 3.7 billion rupees.

He forecast a budget deficit of 3.6 percent of GDP for the year 1997/98 with total expenditure at 22.3 billion rupees and total revenues at 19.00 billion rupees leading to a deficit of 3.3 billion rupees. The 1995/96 deficit was six percent.

Juganauth's MSM alliance ruled for 13 years until it was defeated at the polls in December 1995 by Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam's alliance of the Labour Party and the leftist Mauritius Militant Movement.
Economist Pierre Yin said the budget would not boost the island's development. "The budget has given some good signals, but it does not constitute a boosting budget," he said.
Yin said it focused on economic growth and on quantitative objectives such as growth, inflation, savings and investment, but made no provision for unemployment.
There would be growth in key sectors such as tourism, sugar and the export processing zone, both offshore and freeport, Yin said.

"But all these will be done without job creation and possibly with an important number of redundancies I forecast that by the year 2000 there will be 80,000 unemployed people," he added. No current employment figures were available.
Economist Xavier-Luc Duval said government offered no real remedy to the unemployment issue through its 1997/98 budget.
"It's such a cautious budget that it fails to address many of the areas that the population was expected from a government ruling with a full majority," said Duval.
The investment climate was deteriorating sharply because government was insufficiently pro-active in welcoming foreign investors, he said.
